title: Chapter 198 – First Waking Day
html:
[The Long Gallery of the Sixth Door – Tian Mo]

Tian Mo has carried the dead down seven hundred and one steps, and he has never once been afraid of the stair. He is afraid of it this morning.

He stands at the top with his stone hand on the rail and looks down the long spiral into the blue light of the Dock, and the old fear comes up through his boots like cold water. It is not a fear of falling. It is a fear of being asked a question he cannot answer. For six hundred years the Warden of the Stair has had one duty, and it was a simple one: keep the sleepers safe, keep the door shut, keep the lamps lit. Today he is to open the door a little way and let a thousand people walk through it, and every one of them will want to know where they are.

"You are muttering," says Bell.

"I am not."

"You are moving your lips." She comes up the last flight behind him, small and brisk, with a basket of folded blankets on her hip. "Which is the same as muttering, for a man who does not speak."

"I speak."

"Twice a week. Both times to complain about the soup."

He opens his mouth to protest, and shuts it, because she is right. The corners of her eyes crinkle. She sets down the basket and looks past him at the stair, at the blue light, at the faint fine mist that rises from the Hall's depths every morning when the lamps are trimmed. She is quiet for a moment.

"I was afraid, too," she says. "Last night. I did not sleep. I kept thinking: what if the first one wakes and screams?"

"And if she does?"

"Then I will hold her hand, I suppose." A small shrug. "There is nothing else to do. You cannot make a person unafraid. You can only be there while she is."

He considers this. It has the dry, plain sound of a thing that is true. He lifts his stone hand from the rail and flexes it, slowly, the way a man tests a bridge before he crosses.

"Then we go down," he says.

"We go down," agrees Bell. "Carry the blankets. You have an arm for it."

* * *

The Long Gallery is a quarter mile of white stone, and every foot of it has been scrubbed.

He sees that at once. The floor shines. The benches along the walls have been wiped and set out in rows, with a folded quilt on each. Qinghe's kitchen has sent forty kettles, hung on a long iron rack above a trench of coals, and the smell of barley and onion hangs warm and thick in the air. At the far end, behind a screen of woven rush, six of the Seven sit on a long bench with their hands folded, as solemn as a row of owls. Their gowns are brushed. Their hair is combed. Tao has been given a wooden spoon to hold, as a badge.

The sleepers are on the other side of a wall.

That is the arrangement Cheng Hui devised, and Tian Mo thinks it a wise one. The wall is not stone but a curtain of pale gauze, hung from the vault, and behind it, in the half-light, the first thousand lie in their beds in tidy rows, each with a lamp at the head. They are the ones who said yes. Hai Ren has made a list in her careful hand, and Zhao has copied it into the Roll, and each name is attached to a lamp. A thousand lamps. A thousand beds. A thousand people who are going to open their eyes into a world they do not know.

"Warden."

It is Cheng Hui, at his elbow, very white. The boy is wearing a formal gown for the occasion, borrowed from Zhao and several sizes too wide. His hair is parted with a ruler. He holds a slate in both hands and looks as though he would give a great deal to be elsewhere.

"You are ready?" says Tian Mo.

"No."

"Good. That is the right answer."

"Is it?"

"I have never seen a man who was ready." He lays a heavy stone hand on the boy's shoulder, with care. "Say the order."

Cheng Hui swallows. "First, the call. Mei and the Nine ask the Hall to wake. Second, the threads loosen. One bed at a time, over an hour, so that no one wakes alone. Third..." He glances at the slate. "Third, each person is greeted by a face they know. Or if they know no one, by a Lin. Fourth, they are given water. Then soup. Then a blanket. Then they are asked their name, and whether they wish to stay."

"And if they do not?"

"Then we give them a bed and a door and a promise. They may go back to sleep. They may leave the Hall." He lifts his chin. "It is their choice. We are only the ones who ask."

"Good."

"I wrote it down in case I forgot."

"You will not forget." Tian Mo lets his hand fall. "But it is wise to have it written."

* * *

They begin at the second bell, and for the first hour nothing happens at all.

The Nine sit in a ring at the center of the gallery on nine small stools. Their eyes are closed. Their hands are joined. Between them, on a low table of black wood, burns the golden flame that rose in the Council Chamber, and its light falls on the gauze and on the thousand pale faces beyond it. Mei sits at the ninth stool. She is a faint silver shimmer. Her small hand rests on Jian's, and his rests on Hai Ren's, and the ring runs round the table like a necklace.

Tian Mo stands against the far wall with his arms folded. He has not been asked to take part. He is the Warden, and this is the Nine's work, but he finds he cannot sit. He watches the gauze. He watches the lamps.

At the third hour, the first lamp begins to flicker.

It is a woman near the front, fifty or so, with a broad weathered face and a gray braid over one shoulder. Her lashes move. Her chest rises, once, twice, in a long quivering breath. Her fingers curl on the quilt, as if reaching for something.

"There," breathes Bell. She is at his side, with a cup in both hands. "There she is."

"Go."

"I am going."

She slips through the gauze like a fish through reeds. Tian Mo watches her kneel at the woman's bedside, watches her lay a hand on the broad forehead. The woman's eyes open.

They are a startling blue. She stares at the vault above her, at the lamps, at the swaying curtain. She is silent for a long moment. Then her mouth works, and a thin rasping voice says:

"Is this heaven?"

"No," says Bell, kindly. "It is a hall. You have been sleeping. Do you know your name?"

"Ishan." A pause. "Ishan Vael. Is the war over?"

Bell's hand tightens on hers. "Which war?"

"The one in the south." The blue eyes search her face. "We were at the river. The Bloom was coming. They said, get in the beds. I said I would not. They said it was the only way. I said, then who will hold the line?"

Tian Mo goes very still against the wall.

"Someone held it," says Bell. Her voice is steady, a miracle of steadiness. "They held it for a very long time. You can rest now."

"Who?"

"Many people."

The woman, Ishan, closes her eyes. Tears run into her gray hair, quietly, down both temples. "I was afraid," she says. "I was so afraid. I did not want to leave them."

"You did not. They are here."

"They are?"

"Some." Bell glances back, a brief quick look, through the gauze at the Warden. "One of them stands against the wall."

Ishan Vael turns her head.

Her eyes find Tian Mo, a tall silent figure in a gray gown with an arm of root and stone. He sees the recognition move across her face like a cloud across a hillside. He sees her mouth form a word.

"Captain," she whispers.

He cannot breathe. It has been six hundred years since anyone called him that.

* * *

He remembers her, after all.

It comes back slowly, in pieces, as he kneels beside her bed with his stone hand folded in her warm one. A girl of seventeen with a broad red face and a cavalry saddle, riding in the vanguard on the first day of the retreat from the river. A girl who had laughed at him for his bad horse. A girl who stood next to him at the barricade when the Bloom came over the ridge like a brown wave, and who never once took a step back.

"You grew old," says Ishan, wonderingly.

"A little."

"Your arm."

"It was lost." He turns it in the light, the pale veined stone, the roots that curl round his wrist like ivy. "I have a better one now. It was grown for me."

"Who grew it?"

"A friend." He cannot think what else to say. "A very odd friend. I will tell you later."

"You have time?"

"I have," says Tian Mo, and finds that it is true. "I have a good deal of time."

She smiles. Her hand tightens on his, and the blue eyes close again, not in sleep but in a kind of deep peaceful weariness, like a woman who has set down a pack at the end of a long march. Bell lays the blanket over her. Somewhere behind them, a second lamp has begun to flicker.

* * *

Late in the morning Mei's light begins to fail.

He sees it from across the gallery. The ninth stool is a small pale smudge, and the smudge is thinner than it was at dawn. Her eyes are shut. Her hand lies in Jian's, and Jian's fingers have tightened round it, very slightly, in the way of a man who has felt a candle gutter and is trying not to say so.

Tian Mo crosses the floor in six long strides.

"Child," he says, low.

Mei's eyes open. They are gray and clear and a little glazed, like windows after rain. "I'm fine."

"You are not."

"I'm fine, Warden." She manages a small crooked smile. "It's only the holding. It's like carrying a bucket for a long time. The arm gets tired, but the water stays in."

"How much?"

"Five." A pause. "Four and a half."

"That is not nothing."

"It's four and a half more than last year," says Mei, with a flash of her old stubbornness. "Last year I'd have been at twelve and running. I'm better at this than I was." She squeezes Jian's hand. "Tell him."

Jian does not look at her. His voice is hoarse. "She is right. The Ring takes a day from each of us for every person woken. That is the arithmetic. She takes the same as the rest." He swallows. "It is the leak that worries me."

"I know," says Tian Mo.

"We cannot stop. But the moment she goes below four..."

"Then she stops," says Tian Mo. His stone hand closes on the back of her stool. "I will carry her to the tree myself. You will not argue."

Mei laughs, very softly. "I never argue with you," she says. "You're too tall."

* * *

Nurse finds him at the soup trench in the middle of the afternoon.

He has not seen her in the gallery before. She comes out of the lamplight in her gray apron with her cap askew, holding a ladle she plainly does not know what to do with, and she stops a yard from him and looks at the crowd. Her round face works. Her hands tremble slightly.

"There are so many of them," she says.

"There are."

"They look so alive." She wipes her eyes with the back of her wrist, and the ladle drips on her shoe. "I watched them for six hundred years, Warden. I fed them through the threads. I turned them in their beds. I knew every one by the shape of the sleep. And now they are sitting up and drinking soup, and I do not know what to say to any of them."

"Say hello."

"It is not enough."

"It is the beginning." He studies her. "You are afraid."

"Yes."

"Of what?"

She is quiet for a long moment. Then, very low: "That they will ask me why."

He understands at once.

"Why you did not wake them sooner," he says.

"Why I let them sleep. Why I never once said no." Her fingers tighten on the ladle. "I told myself it was kindness. I told myself the world outside was worse. I told myself Mr. Cole knew best." A shaky breath. "I think the truth is that I was tired, and it was easier."

Tian Mo says nothing. He has stood at the head of the Dock stair for six centuries, and in that time he has told himself many things. He has told himself he kept the door for love of the sleepers. He has told himself he kept it for duty. He has never told himself that it was easier.

"I will tell you what I think," he says at last. "I think you were not the only one who was tired."

"That is no excuse."

"No. It is a beginning." His stone hand rises, slowly, and rests on her shoulder. It is a clumsy gesture, and it is all he has. "The Archivist at the back would tell you that a tired woman who keeps a lamp lit for six hundred years has done more than most. And the sleepers will tell you whatever they like. But you will not know until you ask."

She looks at him. Her eyes are very wet.

"Ask?"

"Take the soup to the old man in the corner," says Tian Mo. "The one who keeps asking what year it is. Say hello. See what happens."

She stares at the ladle. She stares at the pot. Then she squares her shoulders, fills a bowl, and marches off toward the corner like a soldier going to a barricade.

He watches her go. He thinks that he has not smiled in a very long time, and discovers that his face has forgotten how.

* * *

Hai Ren reads the covenant at noon, standing on a bench with a lamp in her hand.

It is not a long document. She wrote it herself, on the night of the vote, in her clear small hand, and Zhao copied it into the Roll with no more than three corrections. She stands on the bench in the hush of the gallery, her bitten fingers white against the paper, and her voice carries through the murmur like a bell.

"To those who have woken," she reads. "You are in the Hall of the Sixth Door. You were asleep for a very long time. You were asked, and you said yes. That is why you are here."

A rustle. Faces turn.

"To those who have not woken. You were asked, and you said no, or you said not yet. We have heard you. Your beds are warm. Your lamps are lit. No one will wake you unless you ask. No one will move you, or hurry you, or tell you it is time. When you are ready, you will say so, and the Nine will hear."

She stops. She swallows. The paper shakes.

"We were kept," she says, and her voice cracks, and steadies. "Seven of us. We were put in beds by people who loved us, who did not ask. We are not angry any more. But we know what it is to be decided for. So that is the covenant of this Hall. Nobody sleeps who does not choose it. Nobody wakes who does not choose it. And nobody, ever again, decides for you."

She lowers the paper. The gallery is perfectly silent.

Then, at the back, a single slow clap begins. It is the old man from the corner, the one who asked the year. He claps with great deliberation, his hands shaking, and tears run down his face into his white beard. Another joins him. Another. In a minute the whole long hall is ringing, hands beating on benches and quilts and knees, and Hai Ren stands on her bench with her face flaming, looking for somewhere to hide it.

"Well said," murmurs Bell.

"She wrote it in an hour," says Cheng Hui, behind them, helplessly proud.

Tian Mo says nothing. He is watching the Archivist's bed, in the dark beyond the gauze, where one lamp still burns bright against all the others.

It is a thought that does not yet belong to him. It will, before the night is out.

By the evening meal there are four hundred awake.

The gallery has changed. By the first meal it was already loud, and now it is louder. What was a quiet white hall is now a low, murmuring tumult of voices. People sit on the benches in their pale gowns with cups of barley soup in their hands and stare about them with the hollow wide-eyed look of the newly born. Some weep. Some laugh. Many do neither, only sit, stunned, running their fingers over the edges of their quilts as though checking that they are real. A little boy of perhaps six has climbed onto a bench and is explaining to anyone who will listen that he is going to be a soldier. An old man in a corner has asked for the third time what year it is, and each time the answer makes him say, softly, ah.

The Lins move among them like a tide. Tian Mo has never seen the clan at work in this way, and the sight lifts something in his chest he had thought long dead. Zhao goes from bench to bench with his ledger, writing names in the Roll of the Living, in good black ink, with a care that makes people stop crying to watch him. Qinghe has set up in the middle of the gallery with a kettle the size of a cartwheel and is serving soup to anyone who stands still. Yue sits with a cluster of young women on the floor, listening, her bandaged hand open on her knee. Kuang, thirteen and solemn, is explaining the Roll to a gaggle of former soldiers, who listen with grave attention to a boy half their age.

And the Seven are everywhere.

They move through the crowd in pairs, quietly, with water and blankets, and wherever they pass the noise softens. Zhen Li kneels to speak with a girl of her own age. Duan Ke, scowling, carries a very old man on his back to a warmer bench. Ao, perched on Cheng Hui's hip, offers his wooden spoon to a woman who is crying, and she takes it, laughing through her tears, and the boy beams.

"They are good at this," murmurs Bell, at his side.

"They had no one to teach them."

"Perhaps that is why." She wipes her hands on her apron. "They know what it is to wake in a place you do not know."

He nods. He does not trust his voice.

At the center of the gallery, on a bench by himself, sits Jian.

The Head of the Lin clan looks very small there, a thin young man with a staff across his knees and a cup of untouched tea. He has not moved in an hour. His face is gray with the effort of the Nine-Ring, and the hand that holds the cup trembles slightly, in a way Tian Mo has learned not to remark on. But his eyes are open and steady, and they follow the Seven across the room with a look Tian Mo cannot name.

Pride, he thinks. And grief. It is the look of a man watching children grow up on a road he has already walked.

* * *

Before the lamps are trimmed for evening, Ishan Vael asks to walk.

She is steadier than anyone expected, a broad weathered woman with her gray braid over one shoulder, and she takes Tian Mo's stone arm without hesitation. They cross the gallery together at the pace of an old horse, past the benches and the soup trench and the knots of murmuring strangers. At the far wall she stops and lays her palm flat against the white stone.

"It is warm," she says.

"The Hall is warm."

"It was not, before." She turns her blue gaze on him. "The beds were cold at the river. We lay in them in rows like salt fish. I remember thinking: if I wake, I want it to be warm."

"It is."

"Then someone listened." Her mouth twists. "I never thought anyone would."

He has no answer. He walks her back across the floor, slowly, as the lamps come up one by one, and when he leaves her at her bench she catches his sleeve.

"Captain," she says. "The line. Did it hold?"

He thinks of a valley under a gray sky. Of a Wall in the snow, and nine hundred children adopted into a Roll. Of a girl made of light holding a door.

"It held," he says. "A long time. And then it was relieved."

Her eyes close in something like peace. "Good," she says. "Good. I was afraid we had left it too thin."

The trouble starts at dusk, and it starts quietly.

A girl comes running. She is one of the Lamplighter's apprentices, ten or eleven, with soot on her cheek and a taper still in her hand. She finds Tian Mo by the soup trench and tugs at his sleeve, and when he bends she whispers, with an urgency that makes his stomach turn, "Warden. Number four hundred and eighteen."

"What of it?"

"He woke."

"That is what they are meant to do."

"No." Her eyes are huge. "He is not on the list."

The cold goes through him from crown to heel.

He goes at once, the girl trotting at his heels, through the press of people to the far end of the gallery, where the gauze hangs untouched. The second thousand. The ones who said not yet, and the ones who said no, lying in their rows behind the curtain with their lamps burning low and steady. There should be no movement here. There has been no movement here all day.

There is one lamp that is bright.

It stands at the head of a bed in the fourth row. The man in it is perhaps forty, lean and dark, with a shaven head and the pale pinched face of a scholar. He is sitting up. His blanket is round his waist and his hands lie flat on his knees, and his eyes, black as pitch, are fixed on the vault with a tight, fierce stillness that makes Tian Mo's hair rise.

"Sir," says Tian Mo. His voice is level. "Can you hear me?"

The man does not turn his head.

"I am the Warden of this place. You are safe. Do you know your name?"

"Perrin," says the man. His voice is a thin dry rasp. "Perrin Ado. Archivist of the Third Division." A pause. "I said no."

"No?"

"I said no. When the girl asked." He turns, at last, and the black eyes lock on Tian Mo's face. "I heard her. A little girl. A silver voice. She asked if I wanted to wake, and I said, no, thank you. I said, not for a long time. I have spent six hundred years in a bed, Warden, and I have made my peace with it. I did not wish to be disturbed."

"I do not understand."

"Nor do I." The man's mouth is white. "That is my difficulty. Because someone woke me. Someone knew my name, and my rank, and the third word of my oath, and called me. And it was not the little girl."

Tian Mo cannot speak.

"It was a man's voice," says Perrin Ado. His hands have begun to shake. "A man I have not heard in six hundred years. He said: Come up, Archivist. There is work."

"Who?"

The Archivist's face crumples, with a kind of terror and a kind of dreadful joy.

"The Tenth," he says. "He said he was the Tenth."

Behind them, at the far end of the gallery, across the long white floor, something falls and breaks. It is a cup. It is a hundred cups. It is the whole sound of a thousand people turning, all at once, to look at the dark.
